summary: Background: Digital decision-support tools, such as the Stroke Triage App (STA), may enhance prehospital triage and clinical decision-making for suspected patients with stroke. However, implementation of decision-support tools and their impact on clinical practice remains insufficiently studied. Objective: This study aimed to investigate paramedics’ experiences with the implementation of the STA in prehospital practice by evaluating the implementation process, the implementation outcomes, and its impact on clinical workflows, while considering contextual factors that may have influenced these dimensions. Methods: STA implementation was evaluated among paramedics in 2 emergency medical services regions in the Netherlands using a sequential mixed methods approach. Actual usage data were extracted from the STA dashboard. Usability, perceived impact, and contextual factors were explored using an online survey and semistructured interviews. Results: Monthly triages ranged from 52 to 153 (median 120, IQR 107‐131). Paramedics’ individual STA use ranged from 1 to 47 times (median 7, IQR 3‐13). Out of 246 paramedics with an account, 76 (31%) completed the survey, and 9 (4%) participated in semistructured interviews. The STA was generally well accepted, supporting structured neurological assessment and communication. Swift technical support, frequent promotion, and use of local ambassadors facilitated STA use. Clinical urgency, poor workflow integration, and limited perceived added value hampered STA use. Users recommended improvements in mobile interface, login features, and additional explanation with triage advice. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that the STA achieved substantial reach and initial adoption within the prehospital setting. However, widespread acceptance did not consistently translate into routine integration in daily practice. Successful implementation depends as much on addressing organizational and human factors as on technical performance.
title: Implementation and Evaluation of the Stroke Triage App Among Paramedics in Prehospital Emergency Care: Sequential Mixed Methods Study

summary: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) represents a significant public health challenge. Its treatment is characterized by high anatomical complexity and a critical need for functional preservation of speech, swallowing, and respiration. While multimodality care, including surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, has substantially improved patient survival, there are still high rates of life-altering toxicities and low response rates to immunotherapy. Current clinical decision-making largely relies on “digital snapshots”—static representations derived from population-based statistics and time point–specific imaging—which usually fail to account for the rapid anatomical and biological change during the course of treatment. Digital twins hold great promise in accelerating scientific breakthroughs and transforming oncology treatment and precision medicine through the creation of high-fidelity virtual patient representations that integrate real-time biological, anatomical, and clinical data. In this viewpoint, we propose 3 interconnected digital twins to establish a conceptual framework for the HNSCC digital twin. These digital twins include the anatomical twin, using virtual surgical planning and augmented reality for geometric precision; the dosimetric twin, using daily imaging and synthetic computed tomography generation for automated adaptive radiotherapy; and the biological twin, integrating deep phenotyping, radiomics, and mechanistic omics to simulate individualized therapeutic trajectories. Beyond acute care, we explore the clinical utility of digital twins in navigating the “de-escalation dilemma” for human papillomavirus–associated disease and improving survivorship through digital phenotyping. With the advent of longitudinal data from medical-grade Internet-of-Things sensors and circulating tumor DNA kinetics, digital twins can serve as active sentinels, detecting functional decline or subclinical events months before clinical manifestation. Furthermore, the implementation of synthetic control arms via virtual populations offers an avenue to accelerate clinical trials and address ethical issues in rare molecular subtypes. Despite this potential, substantial barriers to implementation remain, including profound anatomical instability during treatment, the “black box” nature of deep learning algorithms, and the challenges of multiscale data integration. We provide a technical roadmap for the development of “morphing” digital twins—dynamic systems capable of continuous geometric and biological auditing. By bridging the gap between the macroscopic world of radiation physics and the microscopic world of cellular evolution, digital twins may help shift the management of HNSCC from population-based statistical probability toward more individualized, biologically informed decision-making, with the goal of optimizing HNSCC management while preserving essential patient functions.
title: The Digital Twin Paradigm in Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Opportunities and Challenges

summary: Background: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent critical windows for early neurocognitive intervention, although access to timely, personalized rehabilitation remains limited. Digital health technologies offer opportunities to deliver scalable and individualized cognitive care; however, their successful implementation depends on an understanding of users’ needs, expectations, and barriers. Within a human-centered design (HCD) framework, actively involving end users during the earliest stages of development is essential to ensure that digital rehabilitation is acceptable, usable, and responsive to real-world rehabilitation needs. Objective: This study explores the experiences, rehabilitation needs, perceptions, and challenges of individuals with SCD and MCI regarding cognitive telerehabilitation. The findings are intended to inform the early-stage co-creation and human-centered development of digital rehabilitation solutions. Methods: The study is framed within an HCD perspective to inform the user-centered development of digital rehabilitation solutions. A convergent mixed methods design was adopted to integrate quantitative assessments with qualitative interviews. The semistructured interview explored 4 thematic domains: neurocognitive abilities, network support, user experience and engagement, and digital divide. Twenty-three individuals with SCD or MCI completed the interview together with measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ), and an ad hoc Technological Expertise questionnaire. Qualitative interview data were analyzed using directed content analysis based on 4 predefined thematic domains by 2 independent raters, with interrater agreement assessed using Cohen κ. Qualitative and quantitative findings were subsequently integrated through exploratory Mann-Whitney tests. Results: Twenty-three participants (n=16 female participants; mean age 74.3, SD 7.35 y) were included. Participants reported preserved cognitive performance (MoCA: mean 24.9, SD 3.23), low-to-moderate perceived cognitive difficulties (CFQ: mean 22.4, SD 9.48), and moderate technological familiarity. Qualitative findings revealed memory (n=12, 52.2%), attention/executive (n=6, 26.1%), and language (n=4, 17.4%) difficulties during everyday activities, together with widespread use of compensatory strategies. Participants also described emotional vulnerability, social withdrawal, and feelings of misunderstanding, as well as delayed rehabilitation access despite reporting cognitive concerns to health care professionals. Although most participants had limited prior knowledge of telerehabilitation, they expressed a positive attitude toward home-based rehabilitation, valuing its convenience, flexibility, autonomy, and accessibility when appropriate technological and clinical support was available. Concerns mainly related to limited supervision, technical barriers, and digital literacy. Mixed methods integration showed that perceived technology-related barriers were associated with lower technological competence (median 1.88, IQR 1.69‐2.56 vs median 3.06, IQR 2.75‐3.59; =.002), while no other significant differences emerged. Conclusions: These findings highlight that effective digital rehabilitation should be developed through iterative, user-informed HCD processes that simultaneously address cognitive, emotional, social, and technological dimensions of early neurocognitive decline. Integrated findings highlight the importance of addressing individual needs and incorporating users’ perspectives from the earliest design phases to support usable, engaging, and accessible digital rehabilitation solutions.
title: Early-Stage Co-Creation and Human-Centered Development of Digital Therapeutics for Cognitive Rehabilitation in Early Neurocognitive Disorders: Convergent Mixed Methods Study

summary: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are highly effective for weight management; however, long-term outcomes depend on sustained behavioral engagement. Digital health tools may enhance these behavioral components, but evidence regarding their real-world benefit alongside pharmacotherapy remains limited. Objective: This study aims to evaluate whether augmenting a direct-to-consumer GLP-1 RA program with a behavioral support smartphone app improves weight-loss outcomes compared with medication alone, and to identify which app features are associated with weight loss over time. Methods: A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted using data from 6113 adults (older than 18 years) in Australia who self-enrolled into the Mosh direct-to-consumer weight-loss program between July 1, 2024, and August 13, 2025, with their weight data recorded at baseline and at least 1 other timepoint. Participants received semaglutide or tirzepatide, with optional access to a smartphone app and clinician support. Logistic regression models examined achievement of ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight-loss thresholds at 60, 120, and 180 days. Linear mixed-effects models interacting with app feature use, with linear and quadratic time terms, assessed the association of different features with percentage weight loss trajectories over time. Both models adjusted for medication type, gender, ethnicity, age, and baseline BMI. Results: Participants using the program plus medication had higher odds of achieving clinically significant weight loss than those using medication only. Adjusted odds ratio point estimates for day 60, 120, and 180 (±10) days indicated they were 1.38 (95% CI 1.09-1.75) times to 2.22 (95% CI 1.40-3.45) times more likely to achieve ≥5% weight loss across timepoints, 1.67 (95% CI 1.33-2.10) times to 1.97 (95% CI 1.35-2.90) times more likely to achieve ≥10% weight loss by day 120 and 180, and 1.99 (95% CI 1.26-3.29) times more likely to achieve ≥15% weight loss by 180 days. Mixed-effects modeling demonstrated that progress logging was associated with more rapid weight loss over time (β=.26 percentage-point additional weight lost per 30 days, SE 0.06; =4.46; 95% CI 0.14-0.38; <.001). No other app features were consistently associated with changes in weight-loss trajectories. Conclusions: Augmenting GLP-1 RA treatment with a behavioral smartphone app was associated with a higher likelihood of achieving clinically significant weight loss, although differences in overall weight-loss trajectories were modest. Progress logging emerged as the primary behavioral predictor of improved outcomes. While not causal effects, these findings are consistent with the positive value of integrating digital tools with pharmacotherapy for weight loss.
title: Digital Augmentation of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 for Obesity Management: Retrospective Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> In Vietnam, antibiotic use without involvement of health care professionals is common in the community, despite the legal requirement for a prescription. In low- and middle-income countries, mobile health (mHealth) is perceived as having the potential to improve community health care at low cost. <strong>Objective:</strong> In this study, we aimed to explore the relationship between mobile phone ownership and health-seeking behaviors among caregivers of children aged 5 years or younger to inform the design of an mHealth intervention to improve antibiotic use practices in the community. <strong>Methods:</strong> A convergent mixed methods approach combined a cross-sectional household survey and in-depth interviews (IDIs). We surveyed 450 households with children aged 5 years or younger and interviewed caregivers about their health-seeking behaviors and how they engage with mobile technology to inform their health care decisions and antibiotic use. Qualitative data were collected through IDIs and focus group discussions (FGDs) with a purposive sample of household survey respondents. Data collection was conducted between June and September 2023 at 2 sites: 1 urban and 1 rural area in a northern province of Vietnam. Factors associated with using mobile phones to seek health care information were identified through multivariable logistic regression and thematic analysis. Quantitative and qualitative findings were then integrated to provide contextual insights. <strong>Results:</strong> For the quantitative household survey, 450 of 460 approached households completed the survey. For the qualitative component, 38 of 60 approached caregivers participated in 4 FGDs and 6 IDIs. Almost all households had an internet connection (444/450, 98.7%, 95% CI 97.1%-99.4%). While 80.2% (308/384, 95% CI 75.9%-83.9%) of caregivers used mobile devices to access child health care information, only 27.1% (29/107, 95% CI 19.6%-36.2%) reported using the internet to obtain antibiotic-related information. Older caregivers (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.65, 95% CI 0.43-0.99) and caregivers living in the urban area (aOR 0.45, 95% CI 0.24-0.85) were less likely to seek health-related information online using mobile devices than younger or rural caregivers, respectively. In contrast, a higher level of caregiver education was significantly associated with more favorable engagement in online health information–seeking behavior (aOR 2.73, 95% CI 1.61-4.61). Caregivers demonstrated highly active and intentional online information-seeking behaviors, driven by a strong desire to enhance their knowledge and confidence in making childcare and treatment decisions. Qualitative findings highlighted a need for trustworthy, professionally supported digital health platforms tailored to child health and antibiotic use. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study highlights caregivers’ health care information–seeking behaviors and engagement with digital technologies for antibiotic-related information, demonstrating the potential of mobile phones to support antibiotic-related decision-making and improve antibiotic use practices. These findings provide insights to inform the design of context-appropriate mHealth interventions to support caregivers in making decisions about antibiotic use.
title: Mobile Technology Engagement Among Caregivers and Its Implications for Childhood Antibiotic Stewardship in Northern Vietnam: Mixed Methods Community-Based Study

summary: Background: People living with long-term physical health conditions who are also experiencing subthreshold depression are at risk of developing major depression. In partnership with lived experience experts, clinicians, and software developers, we co-designed CommonGround, an online peer support and psychoeducation platform. CommonGround’s Theory of Change (ToC) was also conceptualized to outline the intermediate outcomes (and associated indicators of whether such outcomes are achieved) needed to improve the mental health of the target population. Objective: This qualitative study, informed by the ToC, aimed to examine the acceptability, usability, and intervention mechanisms of CommonGround and ultimately refine the ToC and corresponding intervention design ahead of definitive evaluation. Methods: A nested qualitative study was conducted within a remote, 12-week feasibility randomized controlled trial comparing CommonGround (intervention group) to signposting to National Health Service (NHS) web pages (control group). Thirty-nine participants were purposively sampled and interviewed within 6 weeks postintervention about their experiences of CommonGround and trial participation. The interview schedule and thematic framework analysis were rooted in a pretrial ToC while being responsive to emergent themes. Results: Evaluating the assumptions and intermediate outcomes (via their indicators) refined our understanding of how CommonGround may support mental well-being. Overall, participants viewed CommonGround as an appropriate, safe space to access self-management information and support from others with a unique shared understanding of chronic illness. However, many participants felt more time was needed for genuine social relations to form and community culture to evolve. Anonymity helped foster a sense of safety but, for some participants, limited the formation of genuine connections. Other factors contributing to low engagement included personal circumstances (eg, limited time). Key suggestions for future development included creating a mobile app that would be easier and more intuitive to access and navigate. Conclusions: CommonGround was considered an acceptable and appropriate space to access peer support, with the potential to positively impact psychological well-being by fostering shared understanding, support, and knowledge exchange. Beyond informing the future evaluation of CommonGround in a definitive trial, the refined ToC identifies the key preconditions, intermediate outcomes, and associated indicators, and assumptions that may underpin the acceptability and usability of digital peer support interventions in achieving their intended outcomes. We also demonstrate how evaluating and refining components of the ToC after the intervention had been implemented in the trial enabled a more nuanced understanding of how and why the intervention may work, for whom, under what circumstances, and informed changes to improve the co-designed intervention. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06222346; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06222346 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/71513
title: Improving CommonGround, an Online Peer Support Intervention for People Living With Long-Term Physical Health Conditions and Subthreshold Depression: Theory of Change–Informed Qualitative Study

summary: Background: Illicit substance use disorders (SUDs) are escalating globally; yet, social stigma and legal barriers restrict access to conventional treatment, and existing research remains skewed toward alcohol and nicotine. Digital interventions incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) offer a discreet, scalable alternative. Objective: This scoping review maps how CBT-based digital interventions for illicit SUDs are designed and delivered across platforms, identifying their theoretical frameworks, functional components, outcome indicators, and reported methodological limitations. Methods: We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) scoping review methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews). Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL) were searched from inception to June 28, 2026, without language, date, or study design limits, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching (July 3, 2026). Eligible studies were empirical primary studies quantitatively evaluating digital interventions incorporating CBT for illicit or nonprescribed substance use; alcohol- or nicotine-only populations were excluded. Three reviewers independently screened and charted all studies, with disagreements resolved by consensus or adjudication. Data were synthesized narratively, with tables, figures, and an evidence gap map. Results: Fifty-six studies published between 2008 and 2026, drawn from 47 distinct participant samples, met the eligibility criteria. Most were conducted in North America (40/56, 71.4%) and used randomized controlled designs (39/56, 69.6%). Polysubstance-using populations were most frequently targeted (32/56, 57.1%), followed by cannabis (13/56, 23.2%), opioids (6/56, 10.7%), and stimulants (5/56, 8.9%). Interventions were delivered mainly via web (24/56, 42.9%) or app (24/56, 42.9%) platforms, and most (49/56, 87.5%) were grounded in traditional CBT, most often combined with contingency management (18/56, 32.1%) or motivational interviewing (17/56, 30.4%). Core functional components included therapeutic intervention (55/56, 98.2%), self-tracking and notification (25/56, 44.6%), reward (24/56, 42.9%), and support and feedback (21/56, 37.5%). Primary outcomes focused on substance use and abstinence (41/56, 73.2%), retention/feasibility (16/56, 28.6%), and mental health status or coping skills (14/56, 25%). Author-reported limitations were predominantly participant-level (52/56, 92.9%), measurement-level (43/56, 76.8%), study-level (34/56, 60.7%), and intervention-level (25/56, 44.6%) domains. Conclusions: Unlike previous reviews confined to a single substance or delivery platform, this review is innovative in mapping CBT-based digital interventions across the full spectrum of illicit substances, including polysubstance use, and in linking their functional components to intended therapeutic mechanisms. It thereby contributes to the development of these technologies and, by synthesizing author-reported limitations, proposes methodological improvements for their future evaluation. At present, CBT-based digital interventions are best positioned as adjuncts that extend the reach and continuity of existing addiction care rather than as stand-alone substitutes for it; substance-specific customization, objective outcome measures, and modular trial designs are needed to establish them as scalable clinical tools.
title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy–Based Digital Interventions for Illicit Substance Use Disorders: Scoping Review of Intervention Design, Efficacy Indicators, and Methodological Gaps

summary: Background: Social media and search engine tech companies, such as Google, use the wealth of data at their disposal to create algorithms to predict suicide risk and provide interventions based on company policies and outputs from these algorithms. Neither the details of these algorithms nor their accuracy in risk prediction are shared with the public; thus, research is needed to verify whether algorithms applied to search engine data can accurately predict suicide risk in a platform user. This paper provides new information about the methodological challenges in studying the value of search engine data for suicide prediction. Objective: This paper describes the study methods and experiences regarding recruiting and retaining participants in a year-long, fully remote prospective cohort study of suicide prediction in people with variable risk of suicide, using Google Search data. Methods: We aimed to recruit 1000 United States–dwelling and English-speaking adults with current suicidal ideation who fell into 1 of 3 categories: participants with a suicide attempt in the past year, participants with a lifetime suicide attempt but not one in the past year, and participants with no suicide attempt in their lifetime. Recruitment sources included online advertisements hosted on various websites, to differing levels of success. Participants completed online surveys and an interview via Zoom to enroll in the study and then were sent follow-up surveys every 2 weeks for the year following initial enrollment. Recruitment was conducted from March 2022 to January 2024, with follow-up data being collected through February 2025. Results: Of 15,120 records created in our Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) survey system, 485 participants were eligible to participate in the prospective year of the study. Recruitment challenges were mainly due to participant dropout across all enrollment time points, with 63.7% (9636/15,120) of the prescreening sample dropping out or refusing. Other issues included the difficulty of downloading Google Search data (446/3277, 13.6%) and not having enough data to meet the inclusion criteria among those who were able to successfully donate (252/3277, 7.7%). Lastly, the study encountered fraudulent behavior, with 489 of 15,120 records (3.2%) being identified as fraudulent over the course of the study. Conclusions: Despite past success with remote clinical research methods, we found that recruitment can be significantly hampered by fraudulent participation, despite the use of state-of-the-art methods to mitigate this problem. Further, the ability to acquire useful Google Search data is extremely challenging and necessitates the use of technical assistance and continuous monitoring of Google Takeout data structure to ensure accurate and complete data donations. The solutions we provide for this type of research should be helpful for future endeavors. However, research is still limited by the barriers to obtaining data from technology companies. These limitations have significant implications in detecting the accuracy and utility of suicide prediction from search engine data.
title: Study Design and Lessons Learned From Using Google Takeout Donations for Suicide Prevention Research: Prospective Cohort Study
